title: Anomaly and outlier detection
summary: From robust z-scores to Isolation Forest, LOF and seasonal residuals, computed by hand on one toy set, then evaluated honestly with precision@k and average precision when anomalies are 1 percent of the data.
outcomes: Explain why mean and standard deviation scores suffer from masking and compute median and MAD based modified z-scores
Compute Isolation Forest path lengths, c(n) and the score 2^(-E(h)/c(n)) for a point
Compute LOF from k-distances and reachability distances and explain when it beats global methods
Detect contextual anomalies in a time series by scoring robust residuals from a seasonal baseline
Evaluate detectors under heavy imbalance with precision@k and average precision instead of accuracy or ROC-AUC alone

lessons.title: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers

blocks.md:
An **anomaly** (or outlier) is an observation that deviates so much from the rest that you suspect a different mechanism produced it: a broken sensor, a corrupted pipeline row, a fraud attempt, a server that is about to fall over. **Anomaly detection** turns that suspicion into a number, a *score*, so that you can rank points and alert on the worst ones.

In the prerequisite course you fit models by minimizing a loss on labeled data. Here there are usually no labels. Anomalies are rare, they come in kinds you have not seen yet, and nobody tags them in advance. So most detectors are unsupervised: they model what *normal* looks like and score how far each point is from it.

scikit-learn draws a distinction worth keeping in mind for the whole course:

- **Outlier detection**: the training data already contains outliers, and you want to find them in that same data. The detector must assume anomalies sit in low-density regions and do not form a dense cluster of their own.
- **Novelty detection**: the training data is clean (or assumed clean), and you ask whether a *new* observation fits it. Here a group of new anomalies may even be dense, as long as it lands where the training data was sparse.

Monitoring a metric against last month's history is novelty detection. Cleaning a training set is outlier detection.

Start with the simplest detector. Ten request latencies in milliseconds: eight are between 12 and 15, and two requests took 95 and 98 ms. The classic score is the **z-score**: how many sample standard deviations a value sits from the sample mean. A common rule flags $|z| > 3$.

blocks.caption: The z-score, and the bound noted in the NIST e-Handbook: with n points no z-score can exceed (n-1)/sqrt(n).

blocks.prompt: Here the mean is 29.7 ms and the standard deviation is 35.2 ms. Using the rule |z| > 3, how many of the ten latencies get flagged?
blocks.reveal:
**None.** The two slow requests score $z = 1.85$ and $z = 1.94$.

Two things went wrong. First, the outliers themselves dragged the mean up to 29.7 and inflated $s$ to 35.2, so they look less extreme. This is called **masking**: outliers hide each other. Second, with $n = 10$ the largest possible z-score is $9/\sqrt{10} = 2.85$, so the rule $|z| > 3$ could never fire on this sample, whatever the data. Even with only the single 95 ms outlier ($n = 9$), its z-score is 2.665, just under the bound of $8/3 = 2.667$.

blocks.md: The fix proposed by Iglewicz and Hoaglin, and recommended in the NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, is to replace the mean with the **median** and the standard deviation with the **MAD** (median absolute deviation: the median of $|x_i - \tilde{x}|$, where $\tilde{x}$ is the median). Both ignore extreme values: you can move almost half the data to infinity before the median moves far. The **modified z-score** is:

blocks.caption: The constant 0.6745 makes M comparable to a z-score for normal data, because the MAD of a normal distribution is about 0.6745 standard deviations. Iglewicz and Hoaglin recommend labeling |M| > 3.5 as potential outliers.

scenes.caption: The raw latencies in ms. Eight cluster tightly around 13; two are far away.
z-scores. The mean (29.7) and standard deviation (35.2) are pulled by the outliers, so the slow requests score only 1.85 and 1.94. Nothing crosses 3.
Robust version: the median is 13 and the absolute deviations from it are shown. Their median, the MAD, is 1.0. The outliers barely move either statistic.
Modified z-scores: 0.6745 x (x - 13) / 1. The slow requests score 55 and 57, far above 3.5, while all normal points stay within 1.35.

blocks.md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

Robust univariate scores still fail on data with structure. Take the 2D point set used in the next two lessons: a dense cluster `a1` to `a6` near (1.2, 1.2), a sparse cluster `b1` to `b5` near (7, 7), and three suspects: `p` = (1.2, 3.2) just above the dense cluster, `q` = (7, 10) above the sparse cluster, and `g` = (11, 1), far from everything.

Score each coordinate separately with z and M. The heatmap shows the result for the three suspects.

blocks.title: Per-feature scores for the three suspects

scenes.caption: z-scores per feature (14 points). Every value is below 2 in absolute size, so the |z| > 3 rule flags nothing.
Modified z-scores per feature. q comes closest with M = 3.31 on y, still under 3.5. The far-away g scores only 1.89 on x, because the sparse cluster at x = 6 to 8 makes x = 11 look ordinary.

p is the clearest local anomaly (2 units from a cluster whose points sit 0.4 apart), yet both of its coordinates are near the middle of each feature's range: |z| < 1. A per-feature score cannot see it at all.

blocks.md: A score is only as good as its model of normal. Mean and standard deviation break under masking; median and MAD fix that for one variable. For data with clusters and local structure you need scores that look at the joint shape of the data, which is what the next lessons build.

blocks.question: A pipeline flags a daily row count as anomalous when |z| > 3, computed over the last 7 days including today. Today the count dropped to zero. Why might it never fire?
options: Because z-scores require normally distributed data and row counts are integers
Because with n = 7 the largest possible |z| is 6/sqrt(7), about 2.27, so |z| > 3 is impossible
Because the MAD of 7 values is always zero
Because a drop to zero is a negative deviation and z only detects increases
blocks.explain: The maximum |z| in a sample of n points is (n-1)/sqrt(n). For n = 7 that is about 2.27, so the rule can never trigger. Use a robust score computed on history that excludes today, or a longer window.

blocks.question: Why does the modified z-score multiply by 0.6745?
options: It converts the MAD into a 95 percent confidence interval
It corrects for small sample sizes the way n-1 does in the standard deviation
For normal data the MAD is about 0.6745 standard deviations, so the scaling makes M read like a z-score
It is the fraction of points the median ignores
blocks.explain: For normal data the median of |x - mu| (the MAD) is about 0.6745 sigma, because 0.6745 is the 75th percentile of the standard normal. Dividing by MAD and multiplying by 0.6745 is the same as dividing by an outlier-resistant estimate of sigma (MAD x 1.4826).

lessons.title: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts

blocks.md: Liu, Ting and Zhou (ICDM 2008) turned the problem around. Instead of modeling what normal data looks like and measuring distance from it, **Isolation Forest** measures how easy a point is to *isolate*. Anomalies are, in the paper's words, few and different, so random cuts separate them from everything else quickly. A point deep inside a dense cluster needs many cuts before it stands alone.

One **isolation tree** (iTree) is built on a random subsample of $\psi$ points:

1. Pick a feature at random.
2. Pick a split value uniformly at random between that feature's minimum and maximum among the points at this node.
3. Send points below the split left and the rest right, then recurse on each side.
4. Stop when a node holds one point, all its points are identical, or the tree reaches the height limit $l = \lceil \log_2 \psi \rceil$.

The **path length** $h(x)$ is the number of edges from the root to the leaf where $x$ lands. No labels, no distances, and no density estimate are involved.

Our 14-point set gives $\psi = 14$ (scikit-learn uses `max_samples = min(256, n)` by default), so the height limit is $\lceil \log_2 14 \rceil = 4$. The figure follows one tree from a seeded scikit-learn forest (`random_state=0`, the fifth of its 100 trees) for two points: the far outlier `g` = (11, 1) and `a5` = (1.2, 1.25) in the middle of the dense cluster. scikit-learn sends $x \le$ split to the left.

blocks.title: One isolation tree: g needs 2 cuts, a5 hits the depth limit

scenes.caption: The root holds all 14 points. A random cut on x at 3.92 separates the left half (dense cluster plus p, 7 points) from the right half (sparse cluster, q and g, 7 points).
Follow g = (11, 1). It goes right. The next random cut, on x at 8.94, puts g alone on the right. Path length h(g) = 2.
Now follow a5. It goes left into a node of 7 points. A cut on y at 0.98 peels off only a6 (y = 0.7), leaving 6.
A cut on x at 1.18 removes a1 and a3, leaving a2, a4, a5 and p. A cut on y at 2.43 then removes p, which is isolated at depth 4.

a5 reaches depth 4, the height limit, in a leaf that still holds 3 points. Instead of growing the tree further, the algorithm adds c(3) = 1.21, the expected extra depth for 3 points. h(a5) = 4 + 1.21 = 5.21.

blocks.md: Path lengths from a single tree are noisy, so the forest averages them over $t$ trees to get $E(h(x))$. The paper uses $t = 100$ trees and $\psi = 256$ by default, and reports that path lengths usually converge well before 100 trees and that detection is insensitive to $\psi$ over a wide range. scikit-learn uses the same defaults (`n_estimators=100`, `max_samples="auto"`).

blocks.title: Path lengths of g and a5 across the first 10 trees

scenes.caption: Each column is one tree. g is isolated after 1 to 3 cuts in every one of these trees.
a5 always reaches the depth limit of 4, and gets the c(size) adjustment for the points still sharing its leaf: values from 5.0 to 6.71. Tree 5 is the one in the figure above.
Averaging over all 100 trees gives E(h(g)) = 2.71 and E(h(a5)) = 5.61. These averages, not single trees, become the score.

blocks.md: A raw path length is not comparable across sample sizes: bigger samples make every path longer. The paper normalizes by $c(n)$, the average path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree built on $n$ points, which has the same structure as an iTree. Here $H(i)$ is the harmonic number, estimated by $\ln(i) + 0.5772156649$ (Euler's constant).

blocks.caption: Equations 1 and 2 of Liu, Ting and Zhou (2008). The same c(.) is the adjustment added at a leaf that still holds several points.

blocks.md:
Worked numbers for our forest: $c(14) = 2(\ln 13 + 0.5772) - 2 \cdot 13/14 = 4.427$.

- $g$: $s = 2^{-2.708/4.427} = 0.654$
- $a5$: $s = 2^{-5.609/4.427} = 0.416$

The paper reads the score this way: $s$ close to 1 means a definite anomaly, $s$ much smaller than 0.5 means safely normal, and if every point scores about 0.5 the sample has no distinct anomalies. When $E(h) = c(n)$ the score is exactly 0.5 for any $n$. These values match scikit-learn's `-score_samples` on the same forest to three decimals.

blocks.title: Anomaly score s against average path length

scenes.caption: For n = 14, c(n) = 4.43. g (E(h) = 2.71) scores 0.654, a5 (E(h) = 5.61) scores 0.416. A path length equal to c(n) gives exactly 0.5.

With n = 256, the paper's default subsample, c(n) = 10.24, so the same path length means a much stronger anomaly. Normalizing by c(n) is what makes scores comparable across subsample sizes. The two marked points only apply to n = 14.

blocks.code:
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest

clf = IsolationForest(n_estimators=100, max_samples="auto",
                      contamination="auto", random_state=0).fit(X)
s = -clf.score_samples(X)        # paper's score s: higher = more anomalous
labels = clf.predict(X)          # -1 = outlier, 1 = inlier
# decision_function = score_samples - offset_; offset_ is -0.5 with "auto"
blocks.caption: score_samples returns the opposite of the paper's score, so negate it. With contamination="auto" the threshold is s > 0.5.

blocks.prompt: With contamination="auto", scikit-learn flags every point whose score s exceeds 0.5. On our 14 points, g scores 0.654, q 0.571, p 0.522, and the sparse cluster's points b1 to b4 score 0.500 to 0.524. How many points get flagged?
blocks.reveal:
**Seven of fourteen**: g, q, p and four of the five sparse-cluster points (b1 scores 0.50004, just over the line). Only b5, the sparse cluster's center, and the dense cluster pass.

Two lessons. First, Isolation Forest is a *global* method: a point in a sparse region is easy to isolate whether or not it belongs to a cluster, so sparse clusters look anomalous. Second, `p`, a clear local anomaly, scores about the same as ordinary sparse-cluster members. The next lesson's method is built for exactly this case.

blocks.md: The fixed 0.5 cutoff of contamination="auto" is not calibrated to your data. In the 1000-point evaluation set of lesson 5 it flags 241 points when only 10 are anomalies. Rank by score, or set the threshold from a review budget, rather than trusting the default label.

Isolation Forest scores a point by how few random axis-parallel cuts it takes to isolate it, normalized by c(n). It is fast (training is O(t psi log psi) and needs no distances), works on a small subsample, and is strongest for global anomalies far from all the data.

blocks.question: You double max_samples from 256 to 512 on a large dataset. Raw path lengths for every point grow. What happens to the score s of a typical normal point?
options: It drops sharply toward 0, because longer paths always mean lower scores
It stays near 0.5 or below, because c(n) grows with n and the score divides by it
It rises toward 1, because more samples make anomalies easier to isolate
It becomes undefined, because the height limit no longer matches
blocks.explain: s = 2^(-E(h)/c(n)). Both E(h) and c(n) grow roughly like log n, so the ratio stays comparable. That normalization is the reason for using c(n) at all.

blocks.question: Why does Isolation Forest cap tree height at ceil(log2 psi) instead of growing each tree until every point is alone?
options: To make anomalies and normal points land at the same depth
Because random splits cannot separate more than log2 psi points
Because it only needs to tell short paths from long ones: anomalies are isolated early, and deep regions get the c(size) estimate instead of more splits
Because scikit-learn trees do not support deeper trees
blocks.explain: Points that survive to the limit are, by construction, the hard-to-isolate normal ones. Their remaining depth is estimated with c(size), so the tree saves work without changing the ranking of anomalies.

lessons.title: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors

blocks.md:
Look again at `p` and `q`. Measured by plain distance, `q` is the stranger one: its 3rd nearest neighbor is 3.00 away, while `p`'s is 1.95 away. But `p` sits about 2 units from a cluster whose points are 0.4 apart, whereas `q` sits about 2 units from a cluster whose points are 2 apart. Relative to its surroundings, `p` is far more out of place.

Breunig, Kriegel, Ng and Sander (SIGMOD 2000) formalized this with the **Local Outlier Factor**: compare the density around a point with the density around its neighbors. The paper calls a point like `p` a *local* outlier, and shows that a global distance-based definition cannot flag such a point without also flagging the members of a sparser cluster.

LOF has one parameter, $k$ (the paper calls it MinPts): how many nearest neighbors define a neighborhood. With $d(p, o)$ the distance between points:

1. **k-distance** of $o$: the distance from $o$ to its $k$-th nearest neighbor. It is a local length scale: small in dense regions, large in sparse ones.
2. **Reachability distance** of $p$ from $o$: the true distance, but never smaller than $o$'s k-distance. This smooths out noise for points that are very close to $o$.
3. **Local reachability density** (lrd) of $p$: one over the average reachability distance from $p$ to its $k$ neighbors.
4. **LOF** of $p$: the average of the neighbors' lrd divided by $p$'s own lrd.

blocks.caption: Definitions 5 and 6 of Breunig et al. N_k(p) is the set of k nearest neighbors (ties at the k-distance are included).
Definition 7. About 1: as dense as the neighbors. Well above 1: much sparser than the neighbors, so a local outlier.

blocks.md: Now compute it with $k = 3$. The numbers below come from a direct implementation of the paper's definitions and match scikit-learn's `LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=3)` for `p`, `q` and `g`. The paper counts every point tied at the k-distance as a neighbor, while scikit-learn always uses exactly k; a1 and a2 have such ties here, so their LOF differs slightly (0.99 by the paper, 0.97 in scikit-learn).

blocks.title: LOF of p, step by step (k = 3)

scenes.caption: p's 3 nearest neighbors are a4, a3 and a5, at distances 1.61, 1.73 and 1.95.
Each neighbor's own k-distance is tiny (0.39 to 0.51) because the dense cluster is packed tightly.
Reachability distance is the larger of the two, so here it is just the real distance. Its average is 1.763, so lrd(p) = 1 / 1.763 = 0.567.
The neighbors' own densities are 2.11, 2.13 and 1.96 (average 2.066): about 3.6 times p's density. LOF(p) = 2.066 / 0.567 = 3.64.

blocks.prompt: q's neighbors are b4, b3 and b5 at distances 1.97, 2.20 and 3.00. The sparse cluster's points have k-distances around 1.6 to 2.2 and lrd values around 0.45 to 0.5. Will LOF(q) be closer to 1 or to p's 3.64?
blocks.reveal:
**Close to 1: LOF(q) = 1.15.** b4 is 1.972 away but its own k-distance is 2.110, so the reachability distance is raised to 2.110 (the smoothing step at work). The average reachability distance is 2.436, so lrd(q) = 0.411. q's neighbors have lrd 0.448, 0.505 and 0.460 (average 0.471), and 0.471 / 0.411 = 1.15.

q is about as sparse as the cluster it sits next to, so it is not a local outlier, even though its raw distances are larger than p's.

blocks.title: Raw distance versus LOF on the same points

scenes.caption: Distance to the 3rd nearest neighbor. A distance-based detector ranks g first, then q (3.00), then most sparse-cluster points (2.1 to 2.2), then p (1.95). p looks less odd than ordinary sparse-cluster points.
LOF with k = 3. Cluster members, dense or sparse, score about 1 (0.94 to 1.06 across all 11). p jumps to 3.64, above even g's 3.27, while q stays at 1.15. LOF adapts to each region's own density.

blocks.md:
Breunig et al. prove that for an object deep inside a cluster, LOF is close to 1, with bounds that depend on how much reachability distances vary within the cluster. For points outside clusters they give upper and lower bounds that depend on the ratio between the point's distances and the neighbors' k-distances, which is the *local* in the name.

Choosing $k$: the paper found that LOF values only stabilize once k is at least about 10 (smaller k can make points of a uniform distribution look like outliers), reports that 10 to 20 works well for most of its datasets, and suggests computing LOF over a range of k values and taking the maximum. Our $k = 3$ is only for hand computation. scikit-learn's default is `n_neighbors=20`, and its guide suggests a larger value (35 in its example) when more than about 10 percent of the data are outliers.

blocks.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor

# Outlier detection: score the training data itself
lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20)          # contamination="auto"
labels = lof.fit_predict(X)                       # -1 = outlier
scores = -lof.negative_outlier_factor_           # = LOF, about 1 for inliers

# Novelty detection: fit on clean data, score only new points
nov = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, novelty=True).fit(X_clean)
new_labels = nov.predict(X_new)
blocks.caption: With the default contamination="auto", the cutoff (offset_) is -1.5 on negative_outlier_factor_, so LOF > 1.5 is labeled an outlier.

blocks.md: scikit-learn's LocalOutlierFactor has two modes. With novelty=False (the default) only fit_predict and negative_outlier_factor_ exist. With novelty=True you get predict, decision_function and score_samples, but the docs warn to call them only on new data: scoring the training points that way gives wrong results, and predict will not match fit_predict.

Two other detectors in scikit-learn are worth knowing by name:

- **One-class SVM** (Schölkopf et al., 2001) learns a frontier around the training data in a kernel space (RBF by default). Its parameter `nu` (default 0.5) is an upper bound on the fraction of training points left outside the frontier and a lower bound on the fraction of support vectors. scikit-learn notes it is sensitive to outliers in the training set, so it is best suited to novelty detection on clean data; `SGDOneClassSVM` is a linear-time variant.
- **EllipticEnvelope** assumes the data are Gaussian and fits a robust covariance ellipse (minimum covariance determinant). It works when that assumption holds and fails on multi-cluster data like ours.

LOF answers a different question from Isolation Forest: not how isolated a point is, but how isolated it is relative to its own neighborhood. Use it when normal data has regions of very different density; pay for it with k-nearest-neighbor searches and a k to tune.

blocks.question: Normal data has a tight cluster (spacing 0.1) and a loose cluster (spacing 5). A new point lands 1 unit from the tight cluster. Which detector is most likely to rank it as anomalous?
options: Distance to the k-th nearest neighbor, because 1 unit is a large distance
Per-feature modified z-scores, because the point is far from the median
Isolation Forest with contamination="auto", because it adapts to local density
LOF, because the point's density is far lower than that of its tight-cluster neighbors
blocks.explain: A 1-unit gap is smaller than the loose cluster's normal spacing, so raw distances and global isolation treat it as ordinary. LOF compares the point's reachability distances (about 1) with its neighbors' (about 0.1), giving a LOF near 10.

blocks.question: Why is reach-dist(p, o) defined as max(k-distance(o), d(p, o)) instead of just d(p, o)?
options: To make LOF symmetric, so LOF(p, o) = LOF(o, p)
To smooth out statistical fluctuations: points very close to o all get the same distance, so tiny gaps inside clusters do not create huge densities
To make LOF equal to the k-nearest-neighbor distance
To guarantee LOF is always at least 1
blocks.explain: Breunig et al. introduce the reachability distance so that for points near o the actual distance is replaced by o's k-distance, which reduces fluctuations in d(p, o). The parameter k controls how strong this smoothing is.

lessons.title: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals

blocks.md:
Metrics in production have rhythm: traffic peaks in the afternoon and bottoms out at night. A value can be perfectly normal at 15:00 and alarming at 03:00. Anomalies that depend on context like this are called **contextual** anomalies, and every detector so far misses them because it ignores *when* a value occurred.

Our toy metric is 28 days of hourly requests per second (simulated with a fixed seed): a daily sine wave from about 60 at 03:00 to about 140 at 15:00, plus noise with standard deviation 3. On the last day two anomalies were injected: 118 at 03:00 (normal for midday, absurd at night) and a spike to 182 at 14:00.

blocks.prompt: Score all 672 hourly values with the global z-score and with the global modified z-score. How many points cross |z| > 3 or |M| > 3.5?
blocks.reveal: **None.** The night anomaly (118) has $z = 0.64$ and $M = 0.44$: it is right in the middle of the overall distribution. Even the 182 spike only reaches $z = 2.87$ and $M = 1.93$, because the daily swing makes the global spread large (standard deviation 28.6, MAD 29). The seasonality is variance that the global score mistakes for noise.

blocks.md:
The fix is to score the **residual**: the observed value minus what is normal *for that time*. The simplest seasonal baseline is the median of the same hour over past days. Here we take the 27 days of history, compute the hour-of-day median, and measure the spread of the historical residuals with the MAD. The MAD comes out at 2.0, which implies a standard deviation of $2.0 \times 1.4826 = 2.97$, close to the true noise level of 3.

Notice the framing: history is the training data and today is new data, so this is novelty detection. None of the 648 historical residuals exceeds $|M| > 3.5$.

blocks.title: The last day, hour by hour

scenes.caption: Raw values for the last day (hours 0 to 23). The 118 at 03:00 is lower than every afternoon value, so it looks ordinary globally.
Baseline: the median of the same hour over the previous 27 days. At 03:00 normal is 60; at 14:00 it is 139.
Residual = raw minus baseline. The daily wave is gone; what remains is noise of a few units, plus 58 at 03:00 and 43 at 14:00.
Modified z of the residual, using the historical median (0) and MAD (2.0): 19.6 and 14.5. Only those two hours exceed 3.5; the largest normal hour scores 2.4.

blocks.md: Real series also drift: traffic grows month over month, and seasonality may have several periods (daily and weekly). The standard tool is **STL** (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS, Cleveland et al. 1990), which splits a series into trend, seasonal and remainder components with local regressions; statsmodels exposes it as `STL(endog, period=..., robust=True)`, where `robust=True` uses weights that downweight outliers. You then score the remainder exactly as above.

Twitter's **Seasonal Hybrid ESD** (S-H-ESD), described by Hochenbaum, Vallis and Kejariwal (2017) and released as the open-source AnomalyDetection package, combines these pieces:

1. Extract the seasonal component $S_X$ with STL.
2. Compute the residual $R_X = X - S_X - \tilde{X}$, using the series median $\tilde{X}$ in place of STL's trend. The paper found that the STL trend can absorb a run of anomalies and create spurious ones in the residual.
3. Run the generalized ESD test on the residual, with the median and MAD replacing the mean and standard deviation. The plain-ESD version (S-ESD) missed anomalies when a large fraction of the series was anomalous, because they inflated the mean and standard deviation.

scenes.caption: Start from the raw metric, which mixes a daily pattern, a slowly moving level and noise.
STL estimates the seasonal component. The paper's variant takes the series median as the stable level instead of the STL trend.
Subtracting both leaves a residual where seasonal and level effects are gone, so contextual anomalies become large values.
Generalized ESD with median and MAD repeatedly removes the most extreme residual and tests it, up to an upper bound k on the number of anomalies (k is at most 49 percent of the points).

blocks.caption: Generalized ESD (Rosner 1983, as given in the NIST handbook): compute R_1, remove the most extreme point, repeat up to r times; the number of outliers is the largest i with R_i > lambda_i. S-H-ESD swaps in the median and MAD.

blocks.md: Anomalies in the history contaminate the baseline. If last Tuesday's outage is in the training window, a mean-based baseline and standard deviation absorb it and become blind to the next one. That is why both the toy baseline here and S-H-ESD use medians and MAD: one bad day out of 27 does not move a same-hour median.

For time series, first remove what is predictable (seasonality and level), then apply a robust score to the residual. The detector is only as good as the baseline: a residual is anomalous relative to a model of normal for that moment.

blocks.question: A dashboard alerts when a metric exceeds its 30-day 99th percentile. It never fires on a night-time surge that doubles normal night traffic. What is the best fix?
options: Lower the threshold to the 95th percentile
Compare each value with a seasonal baseline for the same hour (or an STL fit) and alert on large robust residuals
Switch to a mean and 3 standard deviation threshold over the same 30 days
Apply Isolation Forest to the raw values
blocks.explain: The surge is a contextual anomaly: twice night traffic is still below daytime levels, so any global threshold misses it. Lowering the threshold creates daytime false alarms. Subtracting the expected value for that hour exposes it.

lessons.title: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies

blocks.md:
Suppose you do have labels for a test set. How do you tell whether a detector is good? Anomaly data is extremely imbalanced, and that changes which metrics are honest.

The evaluation set: 1000 points generated with a fixed seed. 600 come from a dense Gaussian cluster, 390 from a sparse one, and 10 anomalies (1 percent) are scattered uniformly away from both. We score it with Isolation Forest (scikit-learn defaults, `random_state=0`), LOF (`n_neighbors=20`), and a naive baseline: Euclidean distance from the overall mean.

Two families of metrics:

- **ROC curve**: true positive rate (recall) against false positive rate (fraction of the 990 normal points flagged). ROC-AUC is the probability that a random anomaly scores higher than a random normal point.
- **Precision-recall (PR) curve**: precision (fraction of flagged points that are anomalies) against recall. **Average precision** (AP) summarizes it.

And the operational one: **precision@k**, the fraction of anomalies among the top $k$ scores, which matches how teams work: an analyst can review $k$ alerts per day.

blocks.prompt: Isolation Forest gets ROC-AUC = 0.988 on this set, which sounds nearly perfect. If an analyst reviews its top 20 points, how many of them are real anomalies?
blocks.reveal:
**8 of 20 (precision@20 = 0.40).** The anomalies sit at ranks 1 to 7, 13, 37 and 95. The top 7 are perfect, then the detector mixes in normal points.

ROC-AUC stays high because the false positive rate divides by 990 normal points: even when the 10th anomaly is found at rank 95, only 85 normal points (8.6 percent) rank above it. Precision divides by what you flagged, and with 1 percent anomalies, a small false positive rate still means most flags are false.

blocks.title: Isolation Forest's top 20, rank by rank

scenes.caption: A marks an anomaly, a dot a normal point. Ranks 1 to 7 are all anomalies: precision@5 = 1.0.
At k = 10, 7 hits: precision@10 = 0.70, recall@10 = 0.70.
At k = 20, 8 hits: precision@20 = 0.40, recall 0.80. The 9th and 10th anomalies only appear at ranks 37 and 95.

blocks.md: Why precision collapses is plain arithmetic. With anomaly rate $\pi$, a detector with recall TPR and false positive rate FPR has precision

blocks.caption: Expected precision from the rates; ROC space never sees pi, which is why the same ROC point can mean very different precision.

blocks.title: Precision as a function of false positive rate

scenes.caption: At pi = 1 percent and recall 0.9, a 1 percent false positive rate already halves precision to 0.48, and 5 percent drops it to 0.15. On a ROC plot all of these sit near the top-left corner.
With balanced classes (pi = 50 percent) the same rates keep precision at 0.9 or higher. ROC curves look the same in both cases; PR curves do not.
At pi = 0.1 percent (fraud-like rates), precision at a 1 percent false positive rate is 0.08: about 11 false alarms per true one.

blocks.md: Davis and Goadrich (ICML 2006) proved that one curve dominates another in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space, yet an algorithm that optimizes the area under the ROC curve is not guaranteed to optimize the area under the PR curve. They also showed that linearly interpolating between PR points is incorrect. scikit-learn's `average_precision_score` therefore uses the step-wise sum below rather than the trapezoidal rule, which its documentation notes can be too optimistic.

blocks.caption: Average precision as scikit-learn computes it: each anomaly found adds 1/10 recall, weighted by the precision at that rank.

blocks.md:
For Isolation Forest: the first 7 anomalies come at precision 1.0, the 8th at rank 13 (precision 8/13 = 0.615), the 9th at rank 37 (0.243), and the 10th at rank 95 (0.105). So $\text{AP} = 0.1 \times (7 + 0.615 + 0.243 + 0.105) = 0.796$.

A random scorer's AP is about the anomaly rate, 0.01 (our random scores got 0.015), while its ROC-AUC is about 0.5. That gap in baselines is why AP is the more readable number under heavy imbalance: 0.8 against a floor of 0.01.

blocks.title: ROC-AUC versus average precision on the same scores

scenes.caption: ROC-AUC: LOF 0.999, Isolation Forest 0.988, distance from the mean 0.734, random 0.509. Both real detectors look almost perfect.
Average precision: LOF 0.924, Isolation Forest 0.796, distance from the mean 0.278, random 0.015. The gap between the two detectors is now visible, and the naive baseline is clearly poor.

blocks.md:
Thresholds deserve the same care. On this set, Isolation Forest with `contamination="auto"` (score above 0.5) flags **241** points to catch all 10 anomalies, because the sparse cluster scores high. LOF's default cutoff (LOF above 1.5) flags 39. Setting `contamination=0.01` simply moves the threshold so that exactly 1 percent of the training points (10) are flagged; 7 of those 10 are real.

scikit-learn documents `contamination` as the expected proportion of outliers, used only to place the threshold. It does not change the scores or the ranking, so ranking metrics like AP and precision@k are unaffected by it.

Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

In practice:

- **Labels are scarce and biased.** Labeled anomalies are often the ones an older system already caught. Keep a held-out, time-ordered test period and expect new anomaly types later.
- **Pick k from capacity.** If on-call can investigate 20 alerts a day, precision@20 and recall@20 are the numbers that matter.
- **Compare to a dumb baseline.** Distance from the mean, or a seasonal residual for time series, is cheap; a complex detector has to beat it on AP.

Under heavy imbalance, judge detectors by ranking quality where you will act: AP and the PR curve for the whole ranking, precision@k for the review budget. ROC-AUC hides false alarms because it divides them by the huge number of normal points.

blocks.question: Detector A has ROC-AUC 0.97 and AP 0.30. Detector B has ROC-AUC 0.94 and AP 0.55 on the same 0.5 percent anomaly test set. Your team can review the top 50 alerts per day. Which should you prefer, and why?
options: A, because ROC-AUC is threshold-free and therefore more reliable
Neither, because both ROC-AUCs are above 0.9 so they are equivalent
A, because AP is undefined when anomalies are below 1 percent
B, probably: its higher AP means anomalies are concentrated at the top of the ranking, which is what a fixed review budget sees; confirm with precision@50
blocks.explain: ROC-AUC rewards ranking anomalies above the bulk of normal points anywhere in the list. AP weights precision where anomalies are found, so it tracks the top of the ranking. With a review budget, the top is all that matters, so check precision@50 directly.

blocks.question: You change IsolationForest(contamination="auto") to contamination=0.01 and retrain with the same random_state. What happens to average precision on the test set?
options: It stays the same, because contamination only moves the label threshold and does not change score_samples
It rises, because the model now knows the true anomaly rate
It falls, because fewer points are flagged
It becomes equal to precision@10
blocks.explain: contamination sets offset_, which only shifts decision_function and predict. score_samples, and therefore any ranking metric computed from it, is unchanged. Only threshold-based metrics like the precision of the predicted labels change.
